pattern.name: Walk two trees together
pattern.question: To compare two trees, what do you compare at the roots, and what is left to compare afterwards?
idea: Two trees are the same when their roots hold the same value and their left subtrees are the same and their right subtrees are the same. The last two parts are the same question on smaller trees.
So write one function with three base cases (both empty, one empty, values differ) and let it call itself on the matching children. Every pair of nodes is visited once.
spotWhen: The statement compares two trees node by node.
The answer for the pair depends on the answers for the left pair and the right pair.
An empty tree is a natural base case.

dryRun.title: p = [1, 2], q = [1, null, 2]
rows: values are equal: compare the left children
only one is missing: return false
the left pair is false, so && stops and returns false
dryRun.note: The values are all equal, but one tree has the 2 on the left and the other on the right. Shape counts.

constraints: Either tree can be empty
Two empty trees are the same
The shape must match, not only the values
Target: O(n) time

approaches.name: Turn both trees into text and compare
approaches.idea: Write each tree as a level-order list with null marks and compare the lists.

approaches.name: Compare node pairs with recursion
approaches.idea: Check the two roots, then recurse on the left pair and the right pair.

why: If the roots differ in value or one is missing, the trees cannot be equal, which is why those cases return false at once. If they match, the trees are equal exactly when both subtree pairs are equal, so the recursion is correct by induction.
Each call looks at one pair of nodes, so there are at most n calls: O(n) time. The recursion goes as deep as the tree is high, so the extra space is O(h).
mistakes: Checking p.val !== q.val before checking for null, which throws an error on a missing node.
Returning true when only one node is missing because the other values "look" the same.
Comparing only the values with a traversal and ignoring the shape.
Using || instead of && for the two subtree results.
variations: Check whether one tree is a subtree of another.
Check whether two trees are mirror images of each other.
Compare them iteratively with a stack, without recursion.

pattern.name: Compare two nodes with crossed children
pattern.question: In a mirror, which child of the left side should match which child of the right side?
idea: A mirror flips left and right. So a node on the left side must match a node on the right side, and their children match crosswise: left.left with right.right (the outer pair) and left.right with right.left (the inner pair).
This is the Same Tree recursion with one change: the pairs of children are crossed. Start the comparison at the two children of the root.
spotWhen: The statement asks for a tree that is a mirror of itself, or whether two trees mirror each other.
The check can be written as a function that takes two nodes.
The answer for a pair depends on the answers for the pairs of children.

dryRun.title: root = [1, 2, 2, null, 3, null, 3]
rows: values are equal: compare a.left with b.right first
the outer pair is false, so && stops and returns false
dryRun.note: Both 3s are on the right side of their parents. For a mirror, one would have to be on the left.

constraints: The tree can be empty; an empty tree is symmetric
Symmetry looks at both shape and values
Left and right are compared crosswise
Target: O(n) time

approaches.name: Level by level with a queue of pairs
approaches.idea: Put mirror pairs in a queue and compare them one by one. w is the widest level.

approaches.name: Recursive mirror check
approaches.idea: mirror(a, b) compares the values and crosses the children.

why: A tree is symmetric when its two halves are mirrors, and two trees are mirrors when their roots match and each child of one mirrors the opposite child of the other. That gives the recursion.
Every node is part of exactly one compared pair, so there are about n / 2 calls. The recursion depth is at most the height of the tree.
mistakes: Comparing a.left with b.left. That checks equality, not symmetry.
Checking only the values level by level and ignoring missing children.
Starting the helper with root, root and forgetting that it then needs the null checks to avoid errors.
Forgetting the empty-tree case.
variations: Flip a tree so that it becomes its own mirror image.
Check symmetry with a loop and a queue instead of recursion.
Count how many nodes would have to change to make the tree symmetric.

pattern.name: Carry the remaining target down
pattern.question: You step from a node to its child. How does the sum you still need change?
idea: Instead of adding up the whole path at the end, subtract each node value from the target as you go down. Then at every node the question is "can I make the remaining number from here to a leaf?".

At a leaf the question has a direct answer: is the leaf value equal to what is left? A missing child is not a leaf, so it must return false. The two subtrees are tried with || because one good path is enough.
spotWhen: The statement asks about a root-to-leaf path and a total.
A path is built one node at a time while going down.
You only need to know if a path exists, not list them.

dryRun.title: root = [5, 3, 8, 2, 4], targetSum = 12
rows: remaining = 7, try the left child first
remaining = 4, try the left child first
2 is not 4: return false, try the right child of 3
true passes up through || to the root
dryRun.note: The first leaf (2) fails, so the search backs up and tries the other side. The path 5, 3, 4 adds up to 12.

constraints: The tree can be empty; then the answer is false
The path must start at the root and end at a leaf
Values and the target can be negative or zero
Target: O(n) time

approaches.name: List every root-to-leaf path and sum it
approaches.idea: Collect each full path in an array and add it up at the leaf.

approaches.name: DFS with the remaining target
approaches.idea: Subtract each value on the way down and compare at the leaf.

why: A path from a node to a leaf has sum S exactly when one of its children has a path to a leaf with sum S minus the node value. At a leaf there is only the leaf value to compare. This is true at every node, so the recursion is correct.
Each node is visited at most once, so the time is O(n). Nothing is stored except the call stack, which is as deep as the tree is high: O(h).
mistakes: Returning true when the remaining target is 0 at a node that has children. The path must end at a leaf.
Treating a null child as a leaf. A node with one child is not a leaf.
Returning true for an empty tree with a target of 0.
Using && instead of || for the two subtrees.
variations: Return all root-to-leaf paths that add up to the target.
The path can start and end at any node (going downward).
Return the number of paths, not only whether one exists.

pattern.name: Recurse left, record, recurse right
pattern.question: If you want the left subtree finished before the node, where in the function does the node go?
idea: A tree walk is one function that calls itself on both children. The only choice is when the node value is recorded: before the calls (preorder), between them (inorder), or after them (postorder).
For inorder, record the value between the left call and the right call. Everything in the left subtree comes out first, then the node, then everything on the right.
spotWhen: The statement asks for a traversal order of a tree.
The words left, node, right (or similar) appear in the definition.
For a binary search tree, a sorted list of the values is the goal.

dryRun.title: root = [1, null, 2, 3]
rows: left child is empty: nothing to do first, then push 1
it has a left child (3), so visit 3 before 2
dryRun.note: Node 3 is recorded before node 2, even though it is deeper, because it sits in the left subtree of 2.

constraints: The tree can be empty; then return an empty array
Return the values, not the nodes
Order: left subtree, node, right subtree
Target: O(n) time

approaches.name: Recursion
approaches.idea: Visit left, push the value, visit right.

approaches.name: Iterative with an explicit stack
approaches.idea: Push the left spine, pop a node, record it, then go to its right child. It avoids deep recursion.

why: Inorder is defined as left subtree, node, right subtree, and the recursion follows that definition. Each subtree is handled by the same rule, so every node is recorded after everything on its left and before everything on its right.
Each node is entered once and pushed once, so the time is O(n). The call stack is as deep as the tree is high, which is O(h).
mistakes: Pushing the value before the left call. That is preorder, not inorder.
Forgetting the base case, so the function reads null.left.
Creating a new array in every call and not combining them correctly.
Returning from the helper but forgetting to return the array from the main function.
variations: Return the preorder and postorder traversals too.
Do the inorder traversal with O(1) extra space (Morris traversal).
Return the k-th smallest value of a binary search tree.

pattern.name: DFS that carries the path down
pattern.question: When the walk reaches a leaf, how can it already know the full route from the root?
idea: Give the recursive function a second input: the path built so far. Each call extends it with its own value and passes it to the children. At a leaf the path is complete and can be saved.
Because each call builds its own new string, there is nothing to undo when the walk returns. The only care is the leaf test: a node is a leaf only when it has no children at all.
spotWhen: The statement asks you to list every root-to-leaf path (not just count them).
The route to a node is needed at the node.
The answer is built while going down, not on the way back up.

dryRun.title: root = [1, 2, 3, null, 5]
dryRun.note: Node 2 has only a right child, so it is not a leaf. The path "1->2" is not recorded.

constraints: The tree can be empty; then return an empty array
Only paths that end at a leaf count
Join values with "->", with no arrow at the start or end
Values can be negative

approaches.name: BFS with a queue of (node, path)
approaches.idea: Keep each node together with its path text in a queue.

approaches.name: DFS passing the path text
approaches.idea: Extend the text at each node and save it at leaves.

why: A path text is the parent path plus an arrow and the node value, so passing the text down builds every root-to-node path correctly. A node with no children ends a root-to-leaf path, which is exactly what must be returned.
Building a text of length up to h at each node costs O(h) per node, so the time is O(n × h). The output itself and the strings alive during the walk also take up to O(n × h) space.
mistakes: Saving the path at every node instead of only at leaves.
Calling a node with one child a leaf, which creates partial paths.
Adding the arrow before the root value, giving "->1->2".
Mutating one shared array and forgetting to undo the push when returning.
variations: Return only the paths whose values add up to a target.
Count the root-to-leaf paths without building the strings.
